extracted.intended_audience: aspiring essayists, satirists, and the general literate public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing persuasive, entertaining essays (including fables, satires, stage-like scenes, and serious religious reflections) that give advice, engage readers, and convey morals without offending. Emphasises devices for making instruction palatable and techniques for showing passions and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make advice agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing so difficult as the Art of making Advice agreeable; we look upon the Man who gives it as offering an Affront...Some convey their Instructions to us in the best chosen Words, others in the most harmonious Numbers, some in Points of Wit, and others in short Proverbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linguistic craft to soften instruction: choose felicitous words, rhythmic/poetic phrasing, wit, or concise proverbs. Vary devices to suit audience and occasion so the counsel is received as pleasant rather than offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the oblique manner (fable/parable) to give counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: This oblique manner of giving Advice is so inoffensive...the wise Men of old very often chose to give Counsel to their Kings in Fables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver moral or political counsel through fable, allegory, or indirect story (e.g., the Turkish tale of the Sultan Mahmoud). An oblique presentation makes the instruction less affronting and can move readers (or rulers) to action more effectively than direct reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite reader participation by leaving room for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mind is never so much pleased, as when she exerts her self in any Action that gives her an Idea of her own Perfections...in Writings of this kind, the Reader comes in for half of the Performance; every thing appears to him like a Discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct works (especially satirical or fable-like pieces) so readers can identify correspondences, apply characters/circumstances, and 'discover' meaning themselves. This engagement increases delight and persuasive power (example: Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel succeeded because it let readers exert their wit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show passions and psychological dynamics through staged scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Motions of the Minds of Lovers are no where so well described, as in the Works of skillful Writers for the Stage. The Scene between Fulvia and Curius...is an excellent Picture of the Power of a Lady over her Gallant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic scenes/dialogue to abstract description when depicting emotional manipulation or internal conflict. Let actions, gestures, looks, and speech reveal character and persuasion rather than telling the reader what to feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise maxims and proverbs appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A Speculation upon 'Many a Little makes a Mickle, A Penny sav'd is a Penny got, Penny wise and Pound foolish, It is Need that makes the old Wife trot' would be very useful to the World...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-chosen proverbs and pithy maxims communicate practical wisdom quickly and resonate with popular audiences; they are especially effective for addressing habits, trade, or domestic conduct. Use proverbs where they clarify and reinforce the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct vivid allegorical visions for social satire
rubrics_metrics.description: I would suppose all the unmarried Women in London and Westminster brought to Market in Sacks, with their respective Prices on each Sack...The Prude and the Coquet should be valued at the same Price...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create imaginative, ironic tableaux (scenic 'visions') that invert or exaggerate social practices to expose follies. Pair high and low elements for comic effect and moral insight; aim to make the moral intelligible without needlessly offending the audience (the writer notes being an 'admirer' helps avoid alienation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone and authorial voice to occasion for reflective/serious pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all the Reflections which usually rise in the Mind of a sick Man...there is none more natural than that of his going to appear Naked and Unbodied before Him who made him...I have endeavoured to express in the following Hymn, which I have composed during this my Sickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For solemn or devotional subjects, adopt sincere tone, cite respected authorities (e.g., Dr. Sherlock, Scripture), and allow personal feeling to shape composition (hymn, prayer-like stanza). Serious reflections should be candid and grounded to be persuasive and consolatory.
